stem:
While recording from an axon during a neurophysiology practical, a 26-year-old student delivers a second suprathreshold stimulus 1 millisecond after an action potential begins, yet no second action potential can be elicited no matter how strong the stimulus.

Which of the following best explains this absolute refractory period?

options.label: A
options.text: The axon hillock is busy integrating the first depolarizing signal
options.misconception: Summation at the initial segment is being confused with channel-level refractoriness.
options.explanation: Integration determines whether threshold is reached; refractoriness persists even when a threshold-level stimulus is delivered directly, because inactivated Na+ channels cannot open.

options.label: B
options.text: The sodium-potassium pump has not yet restored the ionic gradients
options.misconception: Gradient depletion is being blamed for a gating phenomenon.
options.explanation: A single action potential moves far too few ions to exhaust the gradients, and the pump works continuously; the block is the closed inactivation gate, not a lack of Na+ gradient.

options.label: C
options.text: Potassium efflux is opposing any further depolarization of the membrane
options.misconception: The mechanism of the relative refractory period is being applied to the absolute one.
options.explanation: K+ leaving the cell explains the later relative refractory period, when a stronger-than-usual stimulus can fire the cell; during the absolute period no stimulus can work because the Na+ inactivation gates are shut.

options.label: D
options.text: Myelin insulates the segment and prevents new channels from opening
options.misconception: Passive insulation is being treated as an active gating block.
options.explanation: Myelin shapes where channels are located but does not silence them; the absolute refractory period exists in unmyelinated axons too, because it is a property of the Na+ channel itself.

options.label: E
options.text: The inactivation gates of the voltage-gated sodium channels are closed
options.misconception: None; absolute refractoriness reflects Na+ channel inactivation.
options.explanation: Timed with the peak, the inactivation gate of each voltage-gated Na+ channel closes and cannot reopen until the membrane returns below about -55 mV, so no new action potential can start regardless of stimulus strength.

context: Learning objective: explain the absolute refractory period. During it, the inactivation gate of the voltage-gated Na+ channel is closed, so no stimulus can trigger another action potential until the channel resets below about -55 mV.
imageCaption: Neuron RMP, threshold AP, refractory period, saltatory conduction, EPSP/IPSP summation.
